Pylori  is considered an independent risk factor to gastric cancer.
The prognosis with early gastric carcinoma (EGC) is good, compared with other gastric cancers.

Cytotoxin-associated gene A (CagA): Injected into host cells via a type IV secretion system, it interferes with cell signaling pathways, promotes inflammation, and is associated with increased risk of gastric cancer.
Transcoelomic (peritoneal) spread: across body cavities, for example ovarian and gastric cancer (Krukenberg tumour).

Differential diagnosis: bleeding oesophageal or gastric varices (portal hypertension), peptic ulcer (NSAIDs, H. pylori), erosive gastritis, Mallory-Weiss tear, oesophagitis, gastric cancer, portal hypertensive gastropathy, and a coagulopathy from liver disease.

ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Gastric cancer is a malignant tumor arising from the stomach lining, often linked to H. pylori infection and chronic inflammation. Early detection improves survival, but advanced disease frequently spreads to the peritoneum.

sections.p: A malignant neoplasm originating from gastric epithelium, confirmed by endoscopic biopsy showing dysplasia or invasive carcinoma.
b: Endoscopy with targeted biopsies is the gold standard
Histology classifies adenocarcinoma subtypes (intestinal vs diffuse)

t.b: Does the patient have malignant cells? Positive histology confirms diagnosis
Is there a mass or ulcer? May suggest cancer when endoscopy unavailable

sections.p: Staging follows the TNM system (AJCC/UICC) and guides treatment choice.

t.b: Is there nodal or distant spread? Detects N and M disease for staging
How deep is the tumor (T stage)? Provides detailed wall layer assessment

sections.p: Chronic gastritis from H. pylori is the leading cause; other risk factors add to the cumulative risk.
b: Diet high in smoked, salted foods

sections.p: Symptoms are often vague early, becoming more specific as the tumor grows.
b: Epigastric discomfort or fullness after meals
Anemia or melena from chronic bleeding

sections.p: Combine imaging, endoscopy, and laboratory tests to stage and assess fitness for therapy.
b: Tumor markers (CEA, CA 19‑9) – not diagnostic but useful for monitoring

t.b: If CT unavailable, use abdominal ultrasound to look for liver lesions
If PET unavailable, rely on CT and clinical assessment

sections.p: Complications arise from tumor growth, bleeding, or obstruction and may be life‑threatening.
Treatment is stage‑dependent; early disease may be cured surgically, while advanced disease requires multimodal therapy.
b: Early (T1‑T2, N0) – endoscopic submucosal dissection or gastrectomy with lymphadenectomy
Locally advanced – peri‑operative chemotherapy (e.g., fluoropyrimidine + platinum) plus surgery
Metastatic – palliative chemotherapy (fluoropyrimidine + trastuzumab if HER2‑positive) and symptom control
Supportive care – nutritional support, iron or blood transfusion for anemia, proton‑pump inhibitor for ulcer protection

sections.p: Surveillance after curative treatment detects recurrence early; primary prevention targets modifiable risks.
b: Endoscopic surveillance every 6–12 months for high‑risk premalignant lesions
Eradicate H. pylori in infected individuals
Limit smoked/salted foods, quit smoking, maintain healthy weight

sections.p: Several benign or other malignant conditions can mimic gastric cancer on presentation or imaging.
Certain tests may be falsely reassuring or alarming; clinicians must interpret them in context.
b: Normal CEA does not exclude cancer; it is only a monitoring tool
H. pylori serology may stay positive after eradication, so repeat testing should be urea breath test
Endoscopic biopsies can miss submucosal disease – consider repeat or deeper sampling if suspicion remains

whenToSeekHelp: Rapid weight loss with persistent anemia

faq.q: Why is H. pylori such a strong risk factor?
faq.a: CagA‑positive strains cause chronic inflammation, atrophy, and DNA damage, creating a pathway to cancer.
Yes, if detected at an early stage (confined to mucosa/submucosa) and treated surgically or endoscopically.
HER2 overexpression occurs in ~20% of gastric cancers; trastuzumab improves outcomes when added to chemotherapy.
